[spoiler=[b]Chatting with communists[/b]][b]Chatting with communists[/b]

When the monarchy fell, the House of Shangguan fled in all directions.

I ended up here in the White Straits, at the humble little kingdom of Thrysmora. It's a quiet life. So quiet, I start to hear voices in my head. Or maybe that's just the echoes bouncing off the hallways whenever I talk to myself, like right now. I do live in a pretty big house after all. 

To distract myself from the horror of being lonely, I chat with people through this funny little hosting site called 笔友 ("Bǐyǒu"). 

It's this odd sort of VPN and email service you can gain access to through a .onion link. I personally never bothered getting into the specifics of how it works, but with it I'm able to easily bypass Qianxun's pretentious firewall and communicate with folks from the homeland. ARENA often uses the service to scrape the Qianxun web for any misleading propaganda news stories into op-eds to shift public opinion. It doesn't work, of course, since it's only ARENA supporters that read ARENA write-ups, but it keeps the princes busy.

As for me, I use it to chat with communists. No, I don't use it to snitch on the whereabouts of my family members or anything like that, I just use it for some casual banter with people who couldn't care less about the supposed "dangers" of Qianxun monarchism. Take this one fellow, Cui Jin, party secretary of the University of Qianxun Project 661. He's a bit of a big deal, being the nephew of General Secretary Cui Fang and all, and yet we regularly chat with each other about how our side of the world's going on. I talk about the Thrysmoran summers, he talks about some ridiculous thesis proposal a student sent in, that kind of stuff.

In this life you'll sometimes run into things you really, really shouldn't be doing, but which you'd do purely for the thrill, the burning feeling of missing out. Sneaking off to a night club with friends was the old school deal, then there were stimulants, or joining up with a shady students' organization with fancy patron links. Maybe it's talking back to your parents for the first time in your life, or asking a crazy question that others would deem completely taboo.

And I, Emperor of Qianxun, the so-called "icon" of monarchism, regularly chat with a communist about how much things suck. And you know what? For some strange and humorous reason, he does too. He never criticizes the MZP directly, but he's extremely good at harshly lambasting virtually every single thing short of it. Cui Jin was a bit of a pragmatic man, you know. Unlike many in the MZP, he never really seemed to care for the expansion of socialism, the Sanguinian Revolution or the Conference of Discussions at Citharo. He didn't even bother making a public statement about success in the Astaniran Civil War or the New Order socialism in Gythena.

He made it perfectly clear in our first chat that if it were up to him, he'd rather just focus on the Qianxun Lakes.

"It's just water?" I asked him one time, incredulous to know a bit more. "I did hear something went down there recently, though."

"Three people went down." He quickly answered in the email, like he was almost expecting me to dismiss his fascinations. "And it's to the best of my knowledge that I perceive whatever happened there not as an accident but as evidence of something terrible."

Many people have died in the Lakes over the years, the majority of them through naval warfare between rival noble families, often inexplicably the result of some violent storm or brilliant wind that swept entire fleets up. Nowadays, it's because of researchers trying to figure out something and suddenly getting crushed, either figuratively from decompression sickness or literally by the sheer force of water pressing down on their bodies while deep below the world.

People say it's called the Lake of Thousand Fathoms 千寻 ("Qiānxún") not just for the sheer depth, but because it's said those who succeed in touching the very bottom are capable of hearing the souls of those who have been trapped beneath the violent currents. The Qianxun Empire under the Shangguans revered the lakes and believed them to be the two eyes of the goddess mother Shennü, but these rituals eventually ended during the Revolution.

Cui, for the most part, seems to take my stories seriously. Like, [i]very[/i] seriously. He'd often begin our chats by trying to follow up on what was discussed the night before. I mean to be fair, I can't blame him. What else can you leave things up to but the supernatural if something strange keeps happening over, and over, and over again? If the lake isn't alive, why does it seem to keep lashing out if people try to screw around with it?

Speaking of which, I did hear from him recently that he wanted to do "something silly". I sincerely hope he isn't using my stories to try and nicely screw around in the Lakes.[/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]A stern mother[/b]][b]A stern mother[/b]

Cui Jin had resolved to nicely screw around in the lakes.

For those needing more info, there are two lakes that collectively are called the "Qianxun Lakes".

In the west is the greater lake, Qianxun Major, managed by Kuanlo College. It's a strange and violent water form, seemingly alive and frustrated by the intrusion of men upon its surface. As for the east, Qianxun Minor, administered by Taihsu College, still and mirror-like, but teeming beneath the serene surface with creatures that could tear apart flesh and bone. So, it was quite a strange dichotomy then for anyone who wanted to explore the lakes.

On the surface (pun completely intended), Qianxun Minor was the safer zone. With even just a little dinghy and some plastic oars, you could traverse the entirety of Qianxun Minor and come out perfectly fine. Yet, if you so much as capsize or even stare too longingly into the mirror reflection of the waters, you'll end up disappearing completely, vessel and all. And so, most researchers brave the storms of Qianxun Major, because beneath the waves is a world that almost seems accepting to human life.

Cui Jin stood by the port of the QNS Kewang research ship. He was clad in a red changshan of the imperial style, which he paired with a magua jacket and fur-lined wooden clogs. If not for the somewhat mawkish hammer and sickle embroidery on his magua's left shoulder, one might've easily mistaken him for a monarchist agitator. Beside him, Zhang Meihui wore something far more sensible. A form-fitting long-sleeved shirt, a legionnaire hat, a pair of waterproof pants, a pair of moccasin boat shoes with siping to grip onto the slippery surface of the ship. For all intents and purposes, it seems that only of the two was actually taking this trip seriously.

"You'll get blown off deck the moment we start to enter the storm, Party Secretary," said Zhang, one hand firmly gripping the railing of the Kewang, the other holding onto her hat as the winds began to pick up.

"Oh I absolutely will." Cui conceded in a blunt deadpan, "But this is what the Princess Imperial said the Shangguans wear during these rites. Red represents the Vermilion Bird of Summer, and the Mother Goddess likes it when you dress according to the occasion."

"And what's the occasion?" she asked.

"We will be performing an offering that the Goddess probably hasn't experienced in over a century," Cui answered.

"... We as in...?"

"We, as in I'm the one who's gonna do it, but you and the crew are also being put into harm's way for the fun of it. Also, to be a witness to what may or may not happen."

As the ship sailed ahead, the world around them began to stir. The great blue skies began to grey as the waves started to rise and rise into great pillars that struck hard against the Kewang's hull. This was the general experience of all voyages that dared to cross Lake Qianxun Major, for at the center of the waterbody existed a strange and anomalous vortex that manipulated both weather events above the lake's waters as well as the movement of debris in the waters deep below.

Then, the ship stopped.

There, flanked on all sides by the brilliant azure lake surface, the Kewang rested, ominously, the once vicious waves now resting, now completely, but leniently so as to afford the crew a moment's respite. The "eye of the storm", or fēngyǎn as it was called. They were now at the very center of Qianxun Major.

"Here we are, Mr. Party Secretary," Zhang said, her tone clearly bordering on exasperation. "So, why exactly do we need to be in the very center of the lake again?"

"It's in the stories told by the Princess Imperial." Cui began, "The Shangguans apparently braved the storms in flat-bottomed junks every eight years to appease the local water goddess, Shennü. The last time anyone ever bothered going to the dead center of this lake for this ritual was in 1898, so... we have a backlog of 16 rituals to catch up on."

"Yes, but [i]why[/i] do we need to be dead center is the question."

"That one, even the Princess doesn't know. All she could say was that Shennü only accepts offerings here."

Which was a strange thing, to be so picky over the venue, and for what? A wicker basket, upon which were a few traditional cash coins for good luck, some rice cakes, a brass figurine of the Buddha, a talisman, and three incense sticks. And yet, for whatever reason, it was only here, in the center of the great azure, that the Voice began to stir for them, as though it was perfectly cognizant of their purpose.

This "Voice", as it was called, was not really a voice at all, or at least those who attempted to describe it made so using words that could not have possibly described a human tongue. It was a sometimes soothing, but often unnerving foreboding, a strange humming pitched high like the chirping birds of a somber early morning day, and ever-present, not necessarily emanating from a single source but rather enveloping its listeners into a blanket of its own mysterious chants, like a song from a dead land that had emerged out of the waters and was now being sung to those that happen to pass by in lament.

"... I think... I hear someone?..." Zhang said, warily looking behind her to see no one. "Is this...?"

"Yeah, it's the so-called voice in the reports," Cui affirmed, sighing as he took hold of the offerings and walked down into the vessel and towards the diving bell. Zhang walked with him, with the Voice seemingly following their every footstep. The Voice was getting louder and louder, getting more and more agitated as they neared the bell, neared the moon pool that was to commune them directly with the depths below.

"Only up to here, Comrade Zhang." Cui suddenly commanded, stepping into the diving bell by himself. "Seal it nice and tight."

"Please don't die down there, Mr. Party Secretary."

"Oh relax. Even if I do die, you'll only have to deal with my uncle's wrath for having accompanied me here."

"Yeah, thanks, bastard..."

Zhang shook her head and pulled the door closed. The wheel turned with a series of metallic clicks, with eight separate locking points creating a hermetic seal. Through the thick glass port, Cui watched her give a thumbs-up, then disappear. 

A hiss filled the chamber as the bell began to pressurize. Cui's ears popped. A green light above the door illuminated. The floor beneath him shuddered. Through the thick steel, he could hear the distant clanking of the launch mechanism, the whir of electric motors paying out the umbilical. The bell swayed once, twice, then began its descent.

However, the descent would not last for long. Without proper equipment, Cui was not expected to descend into the deepest reaches of the lake itself, as others have before him. Instead, the bell merely took him a few meters below the surface. There, the locks of the bell disengaged with heavy thunks and swung downward into the depths below. Below him, a circle of water lay perfectly still, held at bay by the air pressure inside the bell. The moon pool.

Cui knelt at the edge of the moon pool. He took the wicker basket of offerings and carefully placed it in the center of the pool. Then, he spoke quietly.

"Shennü, I, Cui Jin, son of Cui Shang, born in Danxia, now residing at Kuanlo, on this 13th of November 2028, I come before you with offerings to make my plea."

For a moment, nothing. The basket floated on the surface, just below the hatch. Then, the water parted. A sudden, strange, and brief vortex within the moon pool that pulled the basket straight down, as if pulled by an invisible hand.

The Voice that had been within Cui since the beginning of the ritual was now silent. 

That silence was absolute. Cui could hear his own heartbeat, the blood rushing in his ears. He waited, breath held, for something, anything to happen. 

Then, the water in the moon pool began to rise. Not flood, but rising, as if the surface tension that had been holding the water back had suddenly reversed, a dome of water pushed through the hatch, perfectly spherical, defying gravity. He scrambled backward, hitting the far wall of the bell. The dome continued to rise, filling the chamber, surrounding him.

And then it stopped.

Cui sat in the bell, chest-deep in water that was neither cold nor warm. Through the water, through the steel of the bell, through two thousand meters of lake, he could see it. From beyond the moon pool emanated metallic argent filaments of granite, some growing over faintly into parallel formations, others arranged in concentric structures around a central structure that blazed with a golden light, like the central dome of a fine Elseyran temple or sanctuary.

Beneath the great light stood three figures, seemingly busy attending to some incomprehensible purpose. Moments later, as if to have noticed his presence, the three figures suddenly turned towards Cui, their necks twisting into impossible proportions.

Then, the vision was gone.

Cui found himself on the floor of the diving bell, gasping, soaked, alone. The water had retreated. The hatch hung open above the moon pool, which showed only darkness.

Itzak Alparslan stared out of the plane window at the Niu Davikianstad-Anthony Mercer International Airport. He had just completed a twenty-hour flight across the globe from Yzakastan to Wuloosya to participate in some sort of student-exchange program. Allegedly, he was supposed to be the leading student of a wider program; however, the ruddy 20-year-old had no desire to travel abroad, he wasnt adventurous, nor did he really care for Wuloosya. 

However, diplomacy was diplomacy, and he had already heard whispers that his uncle was planning on installing him as the next shah upon the announcement of the current Shahs retirement in twenty or so years. So he decided to grin and bear it, unsure as to what would happen to him.

Stepping off the plane, he would find himself on the concourse, unsure as to what he needed to do or where he needed to go he would seek out a Wuloosyan guard.
